skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: In a random sample of 400 voters in a city, 56% supported a new park. The margin of error for this estimate is 4 percentage points. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A margin of error gives a plausible range for the whole population: $56 \pm 4$, or 52% to 60%.
choices: Exactly 56% of all voters in the city support the new park.
Fewer than 52% of all voters in the city support the new park.
Between 52% and 60% of the voters in the sample support the new park.
It is plausible that between 52% and 60% of all voters in the city support the new park.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: In a random sample of 150 households in a city, the mean monthly electricity use was 210 kilowatt-hours, with an associated margin of error of 12 kilowatt-hours. A second random sample of 600 households from the same city will be selected using the same method. Which statement about the margin of error for the second sample is most likely true?
questions.explanation: Larger random samples produce smaller margins of error, so it will most likely be less than 12. It will not shrink to exactly a quarter (3), because the margin of error depends on the square root of the sample size.
choices: It will be greater than 12 kilowatt-hours.
It will be exactly 12 kilowatt-hours.
It will be exactly 3 kilowatt-hours.
It will be less than 12 kilowatt-hours.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A forester examined a random sample of 150 trees from a forest of 9,000 trees and found that 16% of the sampled trees were infected with a fungus. The margin of error for this estimate is 5 percentage points. Which of the following is a plausible number of infected trees in the whole forest?
questions.explanation: The plausible share of infected trees is $16\% \pm 5\%$, or 11% to 21%. Of 9,000 trees, that is 990 to 1,890 trees, and only 1,200 falls in that range.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: In a random sample of 150 households in a town, 36 households own a bicycle. There are 5,000 households in the town. Based on the sample, about how many households in the town own a bicycle?
questions.explanation: In the sample, $\dfrac{36}{150} = 0.24$, or 24%, of households own a bicycle. For the whole town: $0.24 \times 5{,}000 = 1{,}200$.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: In a random sample of 600 adults in a region, 42% said they ride a bicycle at least once a week. The margin of error for this estimate is 4 percentage points. Researchers plan a new random sample of adults from the same region to estimate the same percentage with a smaller margin of error. Which change would most likely achieve this?
questions.explanation: Larger random samples give smaller margins of error. Surveying only bicycle owners would bias the estimate rather than make it more precise.
choices: Decreasing the sample size to 300 adults
Surveying only adults who own bicycles
Increasing the sample size to 1,200 adults
Surveying adults in a neighboring region instead

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A researcher selected a random sample of 300 adults in a city and recorded the number of hours each spent reading in the previous week. Based on the sample, she estimated with 95% confidence that the mean number of hours spent reading by all adults in the city in that week was between 2.8 hours and 4.2 hours. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A confidence interval estimates the population **mean**, so it gives plausible values for the mean of all adults. It says nothing about what share of individuals fall in that range, and it doesn't pin the mean to exactly 3.5.
choices: About 95% of all adults in the city spent between 2.8 and 4.2 hours reading in that week.
The mean number of hours spent reading by all adults in the city in that week was exactly 3.5.
An adult chosen at random from the city most likely spent between 2.8 and 4.2 hours reading in that week.
It is plausible that the mean number of hours spent reading by all adults in the city in that week was between 2.8 and 4.2.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A random sample of 500 households in a city found that 62% of them water their gardens with drip irrigation. The margin of error for this estimate is 4 percentage points. A second random sample of 2,000 households from the same city will be surveyed using the same method. Which statement about the margin of error of the second survey is most likely true?
choices: It will most likely be greater than 4 percentage points.
It will most likely be less than 4 percentage points.
It will be exactly 1 percentage point, since the sample is four times as large.
It will be exactly 4 percentage points, since both samples come from the same city.
questions.explanation: Larger random samples give more precise estimates, so the margin of error should shrink. It need not be exactly 1 point: quadrupling the sample size roughly halves the margin of error.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A random sample of 400 voters in a city was surveyed, and 56% of them said they support a proposal for a new park. The survey's margin of error is 4 percentage points. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: It is plausible that between 52% and 60% of all voters in the city support the proposal.
Exactly 56% of all voters in the city support the proposal.
Between 52% and 60% of the voters in the sample support the proposal.
Most voters in every city support new parks.
questions.explanation: The margin of error describes the likely range for the whole population: $56\% \pm 4\%$, or 52% to 60% of all voters. The sample's own value is exactly 56%, and nothing supports claims about other cities.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A city has 20,000 residents. In a random sample of 500 residents, 30% said they would use a new bus route. The margin of error for this estimate is 3 percentage points. Based on these results, which is the most plausible estimate of the number of residents in the city who would use the bus route?
choices: Exactly 150 residents
Between 5,400 and 6,600 residents
Between 270 and 330 residents
Between 6,000 and 6,600 residents
questions.explanation: The plausible range is 27% to 33% of all 20,000 residents: $0.27 \times 20{,}000 = 5{,}400$ and $0.33 \times 20{,}000 = 6{,}600$. Choice C applies the range to the sample of 500 instead.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A researcher randomly selected 200 members of a city's public library and asked how many books they had borrowed in the past month. To which group can the results of the survey most appropriately be generalized?
choices: All residents of the city
All readers in the country
Only the 200 members who were surveyed
All members of the city's public library
questions.explanation: The sample was chosen at random from library members, so the results apply to all library members. They cannot be extended to all residents or all readers, who were not sampled, and a random sample is meant to represent more than just itself.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: Two random samples were taken from the same population of 5,000 workers to estimate the average commute time. Sample A had 100 workers and Sample B had 400 workers. Which statement is most likely true?
choices: Sample A's estimate will have a smaller margin of error than Sample B's.
Both estimates will have exactly the same margin of error.
Sample A's estimate will be exactly equal to the population average.
Sample B's estimate will have a smaller margin of error than Sample A's.
questions.explanation: Larger random samples generally give estimates with smaller margins of error, so Sample B, with 400 workers, is likely more precise. No random sample guarantees the exact population value.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: In a random sample of 1,000 voters, 47% said they plan to vote for a certain candidate. The margin of error is 3 percentage points. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The candidate will definitely win more than half of the votes.
Exactly 47% of all voters plan to vote for the candidate.
The candidate will definitely receive less than 40% of the votes.
It is plausible that between 44% and 50% of all voters plan to vote for the candidate, so the data do not show that a majority supports the candidate.
questions.explanation: The plausible range is $47\% \pm 3\%$, or 44% to 50%, which does not go above 50%. So a majority is not supported, but neither is an exact value or a figure below 40%.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A town surveyed a random sample of 400 of its residents and found that $62\%$ of them support building a new park. The margin of error for this estimate is $4\%$. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Exactly $62\%$ of all residents of the town support building the park.
Between $58\%$ and $66\%$ of the 400 residents in the sample support building the park.
The park will definitely be built because most residents support it.
It is plausible that between $58\%$ and $66\%$ of all residents of the town support building the park.
questions.explanation: A margin of error gives a plausible range for the whole population: $62\% \pm 4\%$, or $58\%$ to $66\%$ of all residents. For the sample itself the value is exactly $62\%$, so choice B is wrong, and A ignores the margin of error.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: Two towns each surveyed a random sample of residents about a proposed bus line. In Town A, $52\%$ of those surveyed favored the proposal, with a margin of error of $3\%$. In Town B, $47\%$ favored it, with a margin of error of $4\%$. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: A greater proportion of all residents in Town A favor the proposal than in Town B.
The data do not establish which town has the greater proportion of residents who favor the proposal.
A greater proportion of all residents in Town B favor the proposal than in Town A.
Town B's larger margin of error shows that its sample was larger than Town A's.
questions.explanation: The plausible ranges are $49\%$ to $55\%$ for Town A and $43\%$ to $51\%$ for Town B. They overlap, so either town could have the higher true proportion. A larger margin of error usually means a **smaller** sample, so D is wrong.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A random sample of $400$ students at a large university found that $62\%$ of them use the campus library at least once a week, with a margin of error of $4\%$. Which statement is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Exactly $62\%$ of all students at the university use the library at least once a week.
It is plausible that between $58\%$ and $66\%$ of all students at the university use the library at least once a week.
At most $4\%$ of students at the university never use the library.
The sample should have included every student at the university.
questions.explanation: A margin of error gives a plausible range for the whole population: $62\% \pm 4\%$, or $58\%$ to $66\%$. A sample cannot give an exact value.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: An inspector checked a sample of $330$ scales selected at random from a population of $8{,}000$ scales to estimate what percentage of the $8{,}000$ scales were inaccurate. From this sample, the inspector estimated that $7\%$ of the $8{,}000$ scales were inaccurate, with an associated margin of error of $2.8\%$. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: It is plausible that between $336$ and $784$ of the scales in the population are inaccurate.
It is plausible that fewer than $336$ of the scales in the population are inaccurate.
Exactly $560$ of the scales in the population are inaccurate.
It is plausible that more than $784$ of the scales in the population are inaccurate.
questions.explanation: The plausible range is $7\% \pm 2.8\%$, or $4.2\%$ to $9.8\%$ of $8{,}000$: from $336$ to $784$ scales.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A research manager selected $2$ random samples of ovens of a certain type to estimate the average amount of time this type of oven takes to preheat to $350^\circ$F. Based on the first sample, the research manager estimated that this type of oven takes an average of $14.2$ minutes to preheat to $350^\circ$F, with an associated margin of error of $1$ minute. Based on the second sample, the research manager estimated that this type of oven takes an average of $14.4$ minutes to preheat to $350^\circ$F, with an associated margin of error of $2.2$ minutes. Assuming the margins of error were calculated the same way, which of the following best explains why the first sample obtained a smaller margin of error than the second sample?
choices: The first sample contained fewer ovens than the second sample.
The first sample contained more ovens than the second sample.
The first sample took less time on average to preheat to $350^\circ$F than the second sample.
The first sample took more time on average to preheat to $350^\circ$F than the second sample.
questions.explanation: Larger random samples give smaller margins of error, so the first sample most likely contained more ovens.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A school has $1{,}500$ students. In a random sample of $200$ of these students, $48$ said they walk to school. Based on this sample, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of students at the school who walk to school?
questions.explanation: $\frac{48}{200} = 24\%$ of the sample walk, and $24\%$ of $1{,}500$ is $360$.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: Based on a random sample of voters in a city, a polling organization estimated that $62\%$ of the city's voters support a proposed law, with an associated margin of error of $4\%$. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Exactly $62\%$ of the city's voters support the law.
It is plausible that between $58\%$ and $66\%$ of the city's voters support the law.
Between $58\%$ and $66\%$ of the people in the sample support the law.
At least $66\%$ of the city's voters support the law.
questions.explanation: The margin of error gives a plausible range for the whole population: $62\% \pm 4\%$, or $58\%$ to $66\%$. It doesn't make the estimate exact (A), and the sample's own value is exactly $62\%$ (C).

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.prompt: A town council selected $80$ of the town's $1{,}200$ residents at random and asked whether they favor building a new park. Of those selected, $20$ said they favor the new park. Based on this survey, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of residents in the town who favor building the new park?
questions.explanation: In the sample, $\frac{20}{80} = 25\%$ favor the park. $25\%$ of $1{,}200$ is $300$.
